extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors and newsroom writers producing news copy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for newsroom language and usage about race, ethnicity, gender, disability, religion and other identity topics to promote inclusive, accurate reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: native-born
rubrics_metrics.description: Use native-born to describe someone who is born in the United States but isn't American Indian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native Hawaiian
rubrics_metrics.description: Known as Kanaka Maoli in Hawaiian, Native Hawaiians trace their lineage and language to Polynesians, including Tahitians, Maoris and Samoans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes federal recognition and distinct Census classification starting in 2000; cultural/lineage background context provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander (U.S. Census definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Census Bureau defines Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander as 'a person having origins in any of the original peoples of Hawaii, Guam, Samoa, or other Pacific Islands.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Census racial categories reflect a social definition of race in the U.S., not an attempt to define race biologically, anthropologically, or genetically; categories include racial and national origin or sociocultural groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (umbrella term)
rubrics_metrics.description: Umbrella term used by the U.S. Census Bureau and other agencies for people tracing roots to original peoples of Hawaii, Guam, Samoa or other Pacific Islands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negro
rubrics_metrics.description: Use African American or black. Do not use to describe a person of African descent. Do not use Negress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term acceptable in organization names and historical references (e.g., National Council of Negro Women). Historically standard in 17th–19th centuries but out of date and potentially offensive since the Black Power movement; provide historical context when used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negro Codes
rubrics_metrics.description: See Black codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negro National Anthem
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to the 1899 poem 'Lift Ev’ry Voice and Sing' by James Weldon Johnson, set to music by his brother and adopted by the NAACP as its official song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in historical context; describes its significance as a representation of resilience and strength of Black people; audio reference provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: neo-paganism
rubrics_metrics.description: Term used to describe contemporary paganism, as opposed to ancient paganism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some prefer 'pagan' or 'neo-pagan' depending on how they view their faith's relation to ancient practices; describes diversity of self-identification within the movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nepali
rubrics_metrics.description: People from Nepal are known variously as Nepalese or Nepali; Nepali is favored in current usage though U.S. press uses Nepalese when referring to those in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nepali can be both a noun and an adjective; use contextually (e.g., Nepali hat, Nepali sari, Nepali government official).

rubrics_metrics.name: neuroatypical, neurodivergent
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms used to describe people of atypical developmental, intellectual and cognitive abilities; used to refer to people who have autism or another developmental difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These terms are used by some in the autism community as alternatives to ableist language; an individual may be neurodivergent while a group can be neurodiverse. Signs listed (from National Institute of Stroke and Neurological Disorders) include developmental milestones and later-life behaviors such as poor eye contact, repetitive language, fixation on routines, intense focused interests, lack of social responsiveness, etc. See neurotypical, neurologically typical.

rubrics_metrics.name: neurodiversity
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept that neurological differences like autism are normal, natural variations in the human brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains origin of the term and notes the Neurodiversity Movement seeks civil rights, equality, respect and full societal inclusion for the neurodivergent; highlights strengths and abilities associated with different neurological wiring.

rubrics_metrics.name: neurotypical, neurologically typical
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms used to describe people with typical developmental, intellectual and cognitive abilities (those not on the autism spectrum or with other developmental differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes common attributes (no noticeable speech delays, better adaptation to change, fewer sensory issues). See neuroatypical, neurodivergent.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Age movement
rubrics_metrics.description: A spiritual movement developed in Western society in the late 1960s linking elements of religion with psychology and parapsychology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes that followers blend mystical elements of organized religions and native practices; movement remains loose and individualized.

rubrics_metrics.name: niggardly
rubrics_metrics.description: Means stingy or miserly; sometimes perceived as insulting because it sounds like the offensive word nigger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with usage because of potential perception despite different etymology.

rubrics_metrics.name: nigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Racial slur; a contemptuous term for a Black person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use unless there is an extremely compelling reason and a supervisor approves it. Notes historical usage and contemporary contested in-group/entertainment variations (nigga); treat with extreme caution and usually avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: niqab
rubrics_metrics.description: A veil worn by some Muslim women that covers all of the face except the eyes.

rubrics_metrics.name: nirvana
rubrics_metrics.description: In English means bliss; in Buddhism, a state of freedom from the cycle of reincarnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives Sanskrit origin meaning 'act of extinguishing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Nisei, nisei
rubrics_metrics.description: Term for the children of Japanese immigrants (second generation); generally applies to American-born children of Japanese immigrants who arrived before the 1924 immigration cessation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains cultural connotations (raised in the U.S., English as first language) and capitalization practices (some institutions capitalize generational terms in certain contexts and lowercase when referring to an individual). See Issei/issei, Sansei/sansei, Yonsei/yonsei.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nollywood
rubrics_metrics.description: West Africa’s film industry, based in Lagos, Nigeria; term derives from Hollywood and Bollywood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains origin story and notes industry is among the world's largest producers of feature films though many are made on small budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: non-binary gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender identities that do not fit within the accepted binary of male and female; people may feel both, neither, or a mixture.

rubrics_metrics.name: non-binary pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the term 'non-binary pronouns' because not all non-binary people use the same pronouns and people of other genders use they/them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead use 'gender-neutral pronouns,' 'they/them pronouns,' or 'pronouns.' See gender-neutral pronouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: non-disabled
rubrics_metrics.description: Term used to refer to someone who does not have a disability; acceptable alongside 'does not have a disability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In general, avoid using 'able-bodied.'

rubrics_metrics.name: nonbinary, non-binary
rubrics_metrics.description: Umbrella term for people whose gender identity or expression falls outside the binary of man and woman; may be considered a trans identity but not always.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible consult the source; note cultural/Indigenous variants like Two-Spirit and Third Gender; encourage asking for pronouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: noncitizen, undocumented noncitizen
rubrics_metrics.description: Noncitizen describes someone living in a place but not a citizen; undocumented noncitizen is someone living without official permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: February 2021 USCIS memo instructs not to use 'illegal alien,' 'alien,' or 'undocumented alien' in communications and to use 'noncitizen,' 'undocumented noncitizen,' or 'undocumented individual' instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: nuts
rubrics_metrics.description: See crazy.

rubrics_metrics.name: obese, obesity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer people-first language when writing about people with obesity: say 'a person with obesity' or 'a person who is overweight' rather than 'obese' as an adjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid judgmental terms like 'weight problem' or 'fat' unless preferred by the subject. Provides preferred/ problem examples (e.g., 'obese people' → 'people with obesity'). References media guidance resources (Rethink Obesity, Rudd Center, Obesity Action Coalition, World Obesity Federation). Updated March 2022.

rubrics_metrics.name: obituaries (LGBT)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting survivors, list partners of gay, lesbian, bisexual or transgender deceased in an order equivalent to spouses of heterosexual deceased.

rubrics_metrics.name: obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)
rubrics_metrics.description: An anxiety disorder characterized by unreasonable thoughts and fears that lead to repetitive behaviors or compulsions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having OCD only if information is relevant and the person has been formally diagnosed by a reputable source; use 'obsessive-compulsive disorder' on first reference and 'OCD' on second; do not use OCD as a casual adjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Okies
rubrics_metrics.description: A pejorative term for people from Oklahoma dating from the Dust Bowl and Great Depression.

rubrics_metrics.name: older (people, adults, individuals, Americans and so on)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred neutral and flexible general descriptor for people in later life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on a survey of age-beat journalists; used as a neutral descriptor in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: om
rubrics_metrics.description: In Hinduism, the mantra of the divine; the ancient Sanskrit name for the absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All mantras begin with om.

rubrics_metrics.name: openly gay/openly lesbian
rubrics_metrics.description: As a modifier, 'openly' is often relevant only when referencing historical figures or to allow for the possibility of previous closeted figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention sexual orientation only when relevant; avoid words like 'acknowledged,' 'avowed,' 'admitted,' 'confessed' or 'practicing' due to inaccuracy or negative connotations. Updated February 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: opposite sex
rubrics_metrics.description: Can be seen as offensive or inaccurate for people who don't identify as male or female or who see gender as a continuum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider using the phrase 'different sex' instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oreo
rubrics_metrics.description: Disparaging term for someone deemed to have shunned their black culture and who 'acts white.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use; see 'Uncle Tom.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Oriental
rubrics_metrics.description: Use to describe things and not people; widely considered offensive when used for people of Asian descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate for terms like 'Oriental medicine' or 'Oriental rugs' but not people. In 2016 HR 4238 replaced 'Oriental' with 'Asian American' in federal laws. Updated February 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthodox Church
rubrics_metrics.description: Any of several Eastern Christian churches rooted in the Middle East or Eastern Europe that do not give allegiance to the Roman Catholic pope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains history (Great Schism of 1054) and worship style; notes ecumenical patriarch of Constantinople as 'first among equals.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthodox Judaism
rubrics_metrics.description: The most conservative of the three major branches of Judaism, strictly adhering to traditional teachings and Jewish law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize in all references; Hasidism is a movement within Orthodox Judaism.

rubrics_metrics.name: orthodox, orthodoxy
rubrics_metrics.description: Term used to denote a clear doctrine implying correct belief according to a particular religion or philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowercase except when referring to Orthodox Judaism or Eastern branches of Christianity or as part of a denominational name.

rubrics_metrics.name: out
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who self-identifies as lesbian, gay, bisexual and/or transgender in their personal, public, and/or professional lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred to 'openly gay' in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: outing
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of publicly declaring or revealing another person's sexual orientation or gender identity without that person's consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered inappropriate by a large portion of the LGBT community; described as potentially based on rumor/speculation. See coming out, closeted.

rubrics_metrics.name: pagan
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, a person who does not acknowledge the God of Judaism, Christianity or Islam and who worships a polytheistic religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many pagans follow Earth-based traditions; note some prefer to capitalize 'Pagan.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Paki
rubrics_metrics.description: A derogatory slang word for people of Pakistani origin; South Asian equivalent of Jap or the 'N word.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use under any circumstances; if quoting someone, treat the word with the same caution as other racial epithets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pakistani languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Urdu and English are the official languages of Pakistan; other languages include Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashtu and Balochi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes Bengali was once an official language until East Pakistan became Bangladesh in 1971.

rubrics_metrics.name: Palestine
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical and contemporary overview of the region that has included current-day Israel; refers to territories under Palestinian National Authority control in the West Bank and Gaza.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains Ottoman and British control history, 1948 changes, and UN General Assembly 2012 upgrade to non-voting observer state; notes ongoing negotiations with Israel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Palm Sunday
rubrics_metrics.description: The sixth Sunday in Lent and the beginning of Holy Week before Easter, marking Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called Passion Sunday though 'Palm Sunday' is the preferred term; explains origin of the name and traditional practices such as the seder reference is for Passover not Palm Sunday.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pan-Africanism
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of political ideologies stressing shared origins and interests of people of African descent, aiming for unity and progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes historical roots, figures like W.E.B. DuBois and Marcus Garvey, and symbolism of flags/colors (red, black, green; sometimes green/yellow/red).

rubrics_metrics.name: pangender
rubrics_metrics.description: A gender identity that can be fluid and might be expressed as both male and female or shift between genders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Falls under the umbrella term genderqueer.

rubrics_metrics.name: pansexual, omnisexual
rubrics_metrics.description: A person whose primary attraction is to a person regardless of their gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes why labels like heterosexual/homosexual may be difficult with non-binary identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: paraplegia/paraplegic
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraplegia is impairment or loss of movement in the lower extremities and torso, typically caused by spinal cord or brain injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid labeling a person as 'a paraplegic'; instead say 'the person has paraplegia.' Note some people may use 'para' in quotes; see quadriplegia/quadriplegic.

rubrics_metrics.name: parent
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper term for a gay, lesbian, bisexual or transgender person raising a child; along with mother and father.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because families are blended, ask subjects which term they prefer when possible; mention a parent's sexual orientation or genetic relationship only when germane. See families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsi, Parsis
rubrics_metrics.description: An ethnic group in India that follows Zoroastrianism; pronounced 'PAHR-see.'

rubrics_metrics.name: partition (1947)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to the division of British India into India and Pakistan, one of the largest forced migrations in history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains geographic details (western Punjab, eastern Bengal), ensuing violence and displacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: partner
rubrics_metrics.description: A commonly accepted term for people in a committed relationship; frequently used in gay or lesbian relationships and for unmarried heterosexuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used where legal marriage does not apply; see husband, lover, relationships for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pashtun
rubrics_metrics.description: An ethnic group primarily along the Durand Line in Afghanistan and Pakistan; approximately 18 million people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes historical political role, and references the Pashtun Taliban's rule and regional autonomy issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: passing
rubrics_metrics.description: When someone appears to be and identifies as a member of another race (e.g., African Americans who passed as white historically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives historical context (e.g., reference to 'Black Like Me').

rubrics_metrics.name: Passover, Pesach
rubrics_metrics.description: Major Jewish holiday commemorating the Israelites' freedom from slavery in Egypt; called Pesach in Hebrew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes timing (late March/April), duration (seven or eight days), and traditions such as the seder and the Exodus story; provides pronunciation guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patel motel
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression based on stereotype that Indians run many hotels in the U.S.; 'Patel' being a common Indian name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes statistic that many U.S. hotels are owned by Indians and that the stereotype arises from that fact; caution about stereotyping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pearl Harbor (metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sparingly as a metaphor or analogy because it may invite stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: people of color
rubrics_metrics.description: A generally acceptable umbrella term to describe people of races other than White.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever possible identify specific racial/ethnic groups; avoid the acronym 'POC'; be aware the term can evoke strong feelings and some dislike lumping distinct groups together. Includes further reading references and updated guidance (Feb. 2021).

rubrics_metrics.name: people-first language
rubrics_metrics.description: Language that avoids defining a person in terms of a disability, typically placing the reference to the disability after reference to the person (e.g., 'a person with a disability').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use people-first language whenever possible; exceptions allowed for awkward sentence structure per the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association.

rubrics_metrics.name: PFLAG
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally Parents, Families and Friends of Lesbians and Gays; in 2014 changed its name to PFLAG to be more inclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes mission and scope (support, education, advocacy) and notes national reach with chapters and members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phillippine names
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically follow Western name order; Spanish names are common; use of nicknames is common; Muslims may follow special naming rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilipino
rubrics_metrics.description: Also Filipino, Pinoy/Pinay; Tagalog usage: Pinoy (male), Pinay (female).

rubrics_metrics.name: pink triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: Now a gay pride symbol; originally the symbol gay men were required to wear in Nazi concentration camps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes historical origin and modern reclaiming of the symbol; lesbians sometimes use a black triangle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polock, Polack
rubrics_metrics.description: A derogatory word for a Pole or person of Polish descent (derives from neutral 'Polak').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid usage; historical context provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: polyamorous
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in more than one consensual intimate relationship at a time; being non-monogamous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not to be confused with pansexual (orientation).

rubrics_metrics.name: polygamy
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of having more than one spouse at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes historical Mormon practice (officially outlawed by LDS in 1890), consequences for members practicing polygamy, and that polygamy is permitted in Islam under certain conditions described in the Quran.

rubrics_metrics.name: post-racial
rubrics_metrics.description: A controversial term describing a society purportedly devoid of racial preference, discrimination and prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
rubrics_metrics.description: An anxiety disorder that can develop after traumatic events; PTSD can be diagnosed a month or more after the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having PTSD only if relevant and formally diagnosed by a reputable source; use full name on first reference and 'PTSD' on second; 'flashback' may be used to denote reliving events.

rubrics_metrics.name: poverty line, poverty threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Represents the level of income deemed adequate to live in a particular place (e.g., U.S. Federal Poverty Level calculated annually).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine eligibility for federal programs and benefits; typically anchored to minimum nutritional requirements plus modest allowance for other needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: poverty violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Fines and fees for petty violations (e.g., fare-hopping, loud music, speeding, driving with suspended license, zoning violations for unkempt property, wearing 'saggy pants,' failure to appear in court).

rubrics_metrics.name: powwow
rubrics_metrics.description: Use only when referring to the title of a specific American Indian event; avoid referring to a general gathering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term evokes stereotypical images; the powwow is a social and sacred celebration involving dancing, drumming, singing; comes from the Narragansett word for shaman.

rubrics_metrics.name: practicing (LGBTQ+)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid this term to describe someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'sexually active' when referring to behavior that is germane.

rubrics_metrics.name: pre-lingually deaf/postlingually deaf/late-deafened
rubrics_metrics.description: Prelingually deaf refers to those born deaf or who became deaf before learning language; postlingually deaf/late-deafened refers to those who lost hearing after learning to speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms are acceptable though explanation may be required for a general audience; references Gallaudet University.

rubrics_metrics.name: preferred pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the term 'preferred pronouns' because someone's pronouns are not merely a preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'pronouns.' 'Preferred pronouns' is appropriate only when someone uses more than one set and indicates a preference. Updated March 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride Day
rubrics_metrics.description: Short for gay/lesbian pride; indicates celebrations commemorating the Stonewall Inn riots of June 28, 1969.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pride events typically take place in June.
